title: Bayline Ship Channel
event: A grounded vessel temporarily blocks the only deep-water channel serving the main container and energy terminals.
why: A ship channel is the navigable water route connecting offshore traffic to inland terminals. Even when the terminals are undamaged, ships cannot reach them when the channel is blocked.
how: Inbound vessels hold offshore, outbound vessels remain at berth, terminal storage fills, and rail and truck transfers lose their planned sequence.
when: The risk grows when anchorage space is limited, storage tanks or container yards are near capacity, or essential cargo has no nearby alternate port.
where: The first effects appear at the channel and terminals, then spread to refineries, warehouses, inland rail yards, manufacturers, and fuel customers.

keyTerms.definition: A maintained water route deep and wide enough for large vessels to reach a port.
keyTerms.example: A container vessel follows a marked channel from open water to a terminal berth.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Several terminals can depend on one channel, making it a shared point of failure.

keyTerms.definition: A designated area where a vessel can wait safely before entering port.
keyTerms.example: A vessel waits offshore at anchorage until a pilot and berth are available.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Anchorage space prevents waiting vessels from creating a navigation or safety problem.

keyTerms.definition: The scheduled period when a terminal is ready to receive and work a vessel.
keyTerms.example: A ship is assigned a twelve-hour berth window for unloading.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A channel delay can cause several vessels to miss their windows and create a longer backlog.

question: Which first response best limits congestion and protects priority cargo?
options: Continue sending every vessel toward the blocked channel
Coordinate safe anchorage, confirm alternate terminal capacity, and prioritize essential cargo
Cancel all regional cargo movement until the vessel is removed
optionRationales: Sending more vessels toward the closure increases offshore congestion without creating channel capacity.
This response controls vessel queues, verifies an alternate before rerouting, and protects the cargo that creates the greatest harm if delayed.
Stopping every movement also blocks cargo that could use safe alternatives or remain moving inland.
takeaway: A blocked shared channel requires queue control, verified alternatives, and priority rules before rerouting.
responsePrinciple: Control the queue, verify destination capacity, and move priority cargo through safe alternatives.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The vessel cannot safely enter the blocked ship channel.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Alternate terminal space and a safe approach were confirmed before the vessel changed course.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: No safe channel or verified terminal capacity is available.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The train is waiting for cargo that cannot reach the terminal transfer point.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Priority cargo is moving through a confirmed alternate terminal and rail interchange.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The rail plan remains tied to the blocked channel and missed berth windows.

cascadeSteps: A grounded vessel blocks the deep-water ship channel.
Inbound and outbound vessels lose access to several terminals.
Terminal storage, rail appointments, and truck transfers fall out of sequence.
Energy, manufacturing, retail, and emergency deliveries are delayed inland.

title: Energy Transfer Center
event: A regional power failure stops pumps, loading equipment, and monitoring systems at a fuel-transfer terminal.
why: Fuel terminals receive, store, and transfer products between pipelines, tanks, rail cars, vessels, and trucks. Power is needed for pumps, controls, communications, and safe loading.
how: Loading stops, trucks and rail cars queue, inventory cannot move to customers, and emergency generators begin consuming the same limited fuel that communities need.
when: The risk increases during extreme heat, storms, grid damage, generator maintenance, or when backup fuel and manual procedures have not been tested.
where: Effects begin at the terminal and spread to fuel stations, hospitals, utility restoration fleets, airports, farms, and emergency operations.

keyTerms.definition: A facility that receives, stores, and moves fuel or another bulk product between transportation systems.
keyTerms.example: Fuel moves from a storage tank into trucks that deliver it to local stations.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Inventory may physically exist at the terminal but remain unusable when pumps and controls fail.

keyTerms.definition: The ability to restart an essential system without relying on the normal electric grid.
keyTerms.example: A tested generator restarts a limited set of terminal pumps after a grid outage.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Limited independent power can restore priority operations before full grid service returns.

keyTerms.definition: A rule for dividing a limited resource among competing needs.
keyTerms.example: Available fuel is assigned first to hospitals, emergency vehicles, and utility repair crews.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Without clear allocation, scarce fuel can be consumed by lower-priority demand.

question: What is the strongest continuity response while normal power is unavailable?
options: Use tested backup power for limited loading and allocate fuel to essential services
Attempt to restart every terminal process at the same time
Release fuel without inventory, safety, or destination verification
optionRationales: This response matches limited backup power to essential operations and directs scarce fuel toward the highest-consequence needs.
Restarting everything may exceed generator capacity and cause another shutdown or unsafe operation.
Unverified releases create inventory, safety, and delivery errors during an already constrained period.
takeaway: Backup power is most useful when it is tested and assigned to a clearly prioritized set of operations.
responsePrinciple: Restore a limited safe process, verify inventory, and allocate scarce fuel by consequence.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Fuel loading is unavailable while terminal pumps and controls are offline.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Tested backup power restored a verified priority loading lane.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The terminal could not safely verify or load the truck.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Aviation and generator fuel availability is being verified during the outage.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Essential aviation support received a confirmed allocation.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: No verified priority fuel allocation reached the air-cargo operation.

cascadeSteps: Grid power fails at the fuel-transfer terminal.
Pumps, loading racks, communications, and monitoring stop.
Fuel trucks and rail cars queue while usable inventory declines elsewhere.
Hospitals, utilities, airports, farms, and emergency fleets face shortages.

title: Bayline Rail Interchange
event: Storm surge and drainage failure flood the rail interchange connecting coastal terminals to inland routes.
why: An interchange sorts and transfers rail cars between routes. Flooding at one interchange can block cargo from several terminals even when inland tracks remain usable.
how: Trains stop outside the flooded area, yards fill, crews lose access, and heavy freight shifts toward roads with less carrying capacity.
when: The risk rises near high tide, during prolonged rainfall, when pumps lose power, or when alternate yards are already receiving diverted trains.
where: The flooding begins near the coast and spreads through port, refinery, warehouse, agricultural, and construction supply chains.

keyTerms.definition: A location where rail cars or trains transfer between routes or railroad networks.
keyTerms.example: Cars arriving from a port are reorganized into trains bound for inland destinations.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: One interchange can connect several cargo sources to a much larger inland network.

keyTerms.definition: A temporary restriction on accepting specified rail traffic when a route or destination cannot handle it safely.
keyTerms.example: A railroad stops accepting new cars for a flooded coastal destination.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A targeted embargo prevents more equipment from entering a growing queue.

keyTerms.definition: Moving cargo between transportation modes such as rail and truck without changing the cargo itself.
keyTerms.example: A container is lifted from a rail car onto a truck chassis.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Transfers can preserve movement, but only when equipment, drivers, roads, and terminal capacity are available.

question: Which response best limits the rail backlog without creating a road-capacity failure?
options: Apply a targeted embargo, verify an inland bypass, and transfer only priority cargo to trucks
Move every rail shipment to trucks immediately
Keep accepting trains into the flooded interchange
optionRationales: This response limits the incoming queue, uses a verified rail alternative, and protects road capacity for the most important loads.
The road network, drivers, chassis, and terminals may not have enough capacity for every displaced rail shipment.
Accepting more trains adds congestion and equipment to a location that cannot process them safely.
takeaway: Diversion works when incoming volume is controlled and each alternate mode is checked for capacity.
responsePrinciple: Stop adding to the queue, verify bypass capacity, and transfer only consequence-based priority loads.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The train stopped before entering the flooded interchange.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: A verified inland rail bypass accepted the priority cars.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The train remains in a growing queue without a confirmed bypass.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Rail diversions are increasing demand for trucks and road space.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Only selected priority loads were transferred to a checked road corridor.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Uncontrolled transfers exceeded available road and truck capacity.

cascadeSteps: Storm surge floods the coastal rail interchange.
Trains stop while yards, crews, and equipment lose access.
Cargo shifts toward inland bypasses and roads with limited capacity.
Energy, agriculture, construction, and retail deliveries arrive late.

title: Coastal Scheduling Exchange
event: A cyber incident makes pipeline nominations, terminal appointments, and fuel-delivery schedules unavailable or untrusted.
why: Bulk energy movement depends on coordinated schedules. Physical equipment may still work, but operators cannot safely move products when quantities, destinations, and timing cannot be trusted.
how: Terminal releases slow, trucks miss appointments, duplicate requests appear, and partners begin making decisions from different versions of the schedule.
when: The risk increases when manual fallback lists are outdated, accounts are shared, vendors use connected systems, or restoration is rushed without verifying data.
where: The initial outage affects the scheduling exchange and then reaches pipelines, fuel terminals, carriers, airports, utilities, and emergency operations.

keyTerms.definition: A scheduled request stating how much product should move through a pipeline and where it should go.
keyTerms.example: A terminal nominates a quantity of fuel for delivery during a defined period.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Incorrect nominations can send the wrong quantity or product to the wrong destination.

keyTerms.definition: Confidence that information is accurate, complete, and has not been changed improperly.
keyTerms.example: Operators compare restored schedules with signed records before releasing fuel.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Available data is not useful when operators cannot trust it.

keyTerms.definition: Confirming information through a separate trusted method instead of the affected system.
keyTerms.example: A known partner confirms a priority delivery through a verified phone number.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A separate channel helps detect false instructions and supports limited safe operations.

question: Which response best preserves essential fuel movement while limiting cyber risk?
options: Use tested manual schedules, isolate affected systems, and verify priority movements through trusted contacts
Accept every automated schedule as accurate once the system reconnects
Share one administrator account across all partners
optionRationales: This response contains the incident while using a tested and independently verified process for essential movement.
Reconnection does not prove that restored schedules are accurate or that the cause has been removed.
A shared administrator account removes accountability and gives excessive access during an incident.
takeaway: Continuity during a cyber incident depends on trusted fallback records, containment, and independent verification.
responsePrinciple: Contain the affected system, verify essential instructions through a separate channel, and restore in controlled stages.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The truck does not have a trusted loading appointment or destination record.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: A verified manual schedule released the priority delivery.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The truck remains staged because the schedule cannot be trusted.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Terminal planning is moving slowly while product schedules are verified.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Verified terminal and cargo records restored controlled movement.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Untrusted scheduling data continues to limit terminal operations.

cascadeSteps: A cyber incident makes energy schedules unavailable or untrusted.
Pipeline nominations, terminal appointments, and truck releases slow.
Partners receive conflicting information and duplicate priority requests.
Fuel availability becomes uncertain for airports, utilities, hospitals, and emergency fleets.

title: Inland Response Hub
event: Evacuation traffic and emergency staging reduce highway capacity around the main inland distribution hub.
why: The hub receives supplies from several transportation modes and sends them to communities. It cannot support those communities when trucks cannot enter, load, or leave on safe routes.
how: Travel times increase, drivers reach hour limits, fuel use rises, loading appointments are missed, and emergency and commercial traffic compete for the same roads.
when: The risk grows when evacuation orders expand, contraflow changes road direction, fuel stations lose power, or destination facilities close without updating carriers.
where: Effects appear around the hub and highways, then spread to shelters, hospitals, stores, utility crews, and communities outside the immediate coastal hazard area.

keyTerms.definition: Temporarily changing traffic lanes so more vehicles can move away from a hazardous area.
keyTerms.example: Inbound highway lanes are converted to outbound evacuation lanes.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Contraflow helps evacuation but can remove normal freight access to coastal destinations.

keyTerms.definition: A controlled location where people, vehicles, or supplies wait until they are assigned and released.
keyTerms.example: Water trucks wait inland until a shelter confirms delivery access.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Staging reduces uncontrolled traffic and prevents supplies from being sent to closed or unsafe locations.

keyTerms.definition: A planned period when a route and destination can safely receive a shipment.
keyTerms.example: A hospital accepts a fuel delivery during a two-hour emergency access window.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Coordinated windows keep critical trucks from competing with peak evacuation traffic.

question: Which action best protects evacuation movement and essential deliveries?
options: Stage trucks inland, confirm destination access, and assign timed delivery windows for priority loads
Send every truck toward the coast on its normal schedule
Stop communicating route and destination changes to carriers
optionRationales: This response separates staging from active routes, verifies that destinations can receive cargo, and uses limited road space at planned times.
Normal schedules can place trucks into evacuation traffic or send them toward closed destinations.
Withholding changes causes failed trips, congestion, and deliveries to locations that cannot receive them.
takeaway: Emergency staging and verified delivery windows protect both public movement and essential freight.
responsePrinciple: Stage before dispatch, verify the destination, and release priority loads during coordinated access windows.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The truck is staged inland while evacuation traffic controls coastal access.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: A verified delivery window opened on an alternate emergency route.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The truck entered congested traffic without a confirmed destination window.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Ground transportation limits are slowing cargo transfer from the inland airfield.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Priority air cargo was matched to a verified ground delivery window.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Urgent cargo remains at the airfield without coordinated ground access.

cascadeSteps: Evacuation traffic and traffic controls reduce normal highway capacity.
Freight vehicles miss loading and delivery appointments.
Drivers, fuel, staging space, and destination access become constrained.
Shelters, hospitals, stores, and utility crews wait longer for essential supplies.
